messages.subject: substituting time for distance
messages.body_plain:
I would like to know if anyone has done the following, and/or if distance
theory supports this application.

I want to measure forest songbird biodiversity in different environments,
and am using high sensitivity, omidirectional (CVX) microphones to record
songbird calls and songs.  The number of species, S, is my index of
biodiversity (where S = total unique species heard), and so S is my object
of interest.  Assume that distance over which birds can be heard on the
recording is known and fixed for a particular stratum (e.g., conifer,
hardwood, and young forest would have different sampling distances).

If I set up microphones to record for 24, 18, 10, 8, 6, 5, 4, 2, 1, .5 hrs,
respectively at randomly placed points, then I would expect some
estimatable detection function for s, i.e., g(S), with more species
detected during the 24 hr recording than during the .5 hr recording.

Can I use g(S) as being analogous to g(y), where y is distance to the
object, whereas S is the number of species heard during the recording
interval?  The 24 hr recording could be equivalent to a radial distance of
0 (or at least, defined as such).  If so, what would be the way to approach
this using the program Distance?  It seems that this problem is related to
catch per unit effort.

Rob Rempel
Research Scientist
Centre for Northern Forest Ecosystem Research
Lakehead University Campus
Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada

messages.subject: Re: Confidence Intervals calculation
messages.body_plain:
> > How did the standard error and 95% CI were calculated on the table 5.5,
> > page 166 of the Distance Sampling book (edition 1993)?

The ci was obtained using the log-based interval on pp88-89, with z=1.96.
(The Satterthwaite method, used in Distance, was not used here.)  se's for
the 'all' option are found by using the fact that the variance of the sum
is the sum of the variances when the estimates are
independent.  e.g. 103.5^2 = 24.7^2 + 100.5^2

Steve Buckland
